listings.name: Cathedral
listings.content: Huge 15th-century church on the site of the former great mosque; richly decorated with the central nave rising to 37 m. An ornate canopy and statue marks the final resting place of Christopher Columbus. If there's a queue for tickets then go to the nearby Church of Salvador (Iglesia del Salvador) and buy a combi ticket. Cathedral admission includes La Giralda, the minaret that is now the magnificent bell tower. Within, you ascend 34 ramps - no need to keep count as they're tallied on the wall - then a last short flight of steps brings you onto the viewing terrace. Church of Salvador: all of its Rocco altarpieces were cleaned and excavations revealed remains from an Islamic mosque and earlier Christian churches, now accessible in the crypt. Unless you like massive cathedrals, the effect is much more impressive.

listings.name: Real Alcázar
listings.content: A beautiful palace in Mudéjar (Moorish) style, built in the 12th century by the Almohad Caliphs. Greatly remodelled and extended in the 14th century by Pedro I the Cruel, its myriad rooms, extravagant architecture, lavish gardens including a maze, with many courtyards, ponds and secrets to be explored, make it a fascinating place to visit. The room where Christopher Columbus's journey across the Atlantic was planned has his coat of arms embroidered on the wall along with those of royalty. The Royal Apartments are open to tours whenever the royal family aren't using them. In the heat of summer the palace is a cool retreat from the sun's glare, and there are night tours Mar-Oct. There are toilets and a cafe within the walls of the site. It gets busy in high season: buy tickets online in advance, and only from the official website. The tourist entrance, "The Lion's Gate", is on the side facing the cathedral and has a large image of a lion above it.

listings.name: Hospital de los Venerables
listings.content: A 17th-century retirement home and hospital for aged and sickly retired priests, restored by the Fundación to preserve an example of Andalusian architecture at its very best. Includes a resplendent Baroque chapel which is highly recommended, as well as the Santa Rufina painted by Diego Velázquez.

listings.name: Torre del Oro
listings.content: A 13th-century tower, the top of which is rumored to have once been covered in gold. It now houses the local maritime museum.
listings.price: €3 adults, €1.50 seniors/students/children 6-14, free children under 6; €2 for audioguide
listings.image: La torre del oro de Sevilla.JPG

listings.name: Alameda de Hercules
listings.content: Authentic and less touristy plaza with local food opportunities.

listings.name: Parque María Luisa
listings.content: Built for the 1929 Iber-Americano World's Fair and now landscaped with attractive monuments and museums.
listings.image: Mudejar Pavillion - Parque María Luisa - Seville.JPG

listings.name: Palacio de Las Dueñas
listings.content: Las Dueñas is a palace belonging to the House of Alba. It was built in the 15th century, with Renaissance architecture style and Gothic-Mudejar influences. The palace is one of the major historic homes in the city. The poet Antonio Machado was born here in 1875. It is also said that Amerigo Vespucci married in this chapel at the beginning of the 16th century. The Palace has a great collection of paintings (Ribera, Luca Giordano, Neri de Bicci), ceramics, antique furniture and other decorative arts, sculptures of Ancient Rome and contemporary (Mariano Benlluire), Flemish tapestries (Willem de Pannemaker), mosaics, and many other pieces of art. An important site for understanding Andalusian customs and history.
listings.price: Fee: €10 with audio guide, ask for reduced prices

listings.name: Plaza de España
listings.content: The site of the Spanish pavilion from the 1929 exhibition: the semi-circle has little ceramic maps of every region of Spain plus images of them and/or their history. It was also used in the filming of the Star Wars prequels. Visit it early in the morning on a weekday to see a long line of immigrants outside one of the government offices it now houses, or visit it right before it closes (officially at 22:00 but likely half an hour later) to see it completely empty and rather eerie.

listings.name: Real Fábrica de Tabacos
listings.content: The main building of the University of Seville was once the Tobacco Factory of Seville, and was constructed between 1728 and 1771 by Sebastián Van der Bocht. Over the main entrance, the triangular façade ends in a statue of La Fama (fame). The tobacco factory was then the largest industrial building in Spain. A monopoly assured high income, which is reflected in the factory's architecture and surrounding gardens. Its chapel and prison complement the main building. In the interior you find impressive stairways, fountains and Patios. It was the setting for the first act of Bizet's opera Carmen. In 1953 the factory was converted into the main building of Seville University. Just behind the tobacco factory, the María Luisa Park borders the historic centre of Seville to the south. Although it's open to the public (as all university buildings are), the building is used for academic purposes. Be respectful: don't venture into closed rooms and disrupt lectures.
listings.image: Real fábrica de tabacos de Sevilla.JPG

listings.name: Palacio de la Condesa de Lebrija
listings.content: The palace is considered the 'best paved house-palace in Europe' owing to its collection of Roman mosaics and marble floors in the 'opus sectile' geometric style, which paved practically the whole of the ground floor. There is also a collection of well parapets, vases, amphora, columns and sculptures of incalculable worth. On the upper floor you can visit the residences previously inhabited by the Countess and her descendants, up to only a few years ago; extremely well-preserved, they are today filled with ornaments and furniture from all over the world, priceless artwork by Van Dyke, Bruegel, Alonso Cano, among others, as well as collections of porcelain and glass.
listings.image: View - Palacio de la Condesa de Lebrija.JPG

listings.name: Casa de Pilatos
listings.content: A 16th-century palace and generally thought to be one of the best in the city.

listings.name: Palacio Arzobispal
listings.content: It is in the historical section of the city and is home to various clergy and the Archbishop. On the outside you only can catch a glimpse of the patio but on the inside there are important works of art.

listings.name: Archivo General de Indias
listings.content: This Renaissance building houses extensive archives relating to the Spanish conquest of the Americas, and is designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Included in the collection are the diaries of Columbus. The archive hosts rotating special exhibits.

listings.name: Metropol Parasol
listings.content: An enormous wooden structure, designed by German architect Jürgen Mayer-Hermann, inspired by the Cathedral of Seville and in the form of giant mushrooms. Known to locals as 'las setas' (the mushrooms), the structure covers the Central Market and the Antiquarium; the top level contains a restaurant and provides some of the best views of Seville.

listings.name: Museo de Bellas Artes
listings.content: Considered by some as the second most important fine arts museum in Spain after the Prado in Madrid. The museum building is a former mercy convent renewed in the 17th century and the 15 exhibition rooms show a comprehensive picture of Sevillian art from the Gothic period to the early trends of the 20th century. The square just outside hosts an open-air art market on Sundays until around 13:30. Plenty of original paintings on local topics, although some not so interesting bits as well!

listings.name: Museo Arqueológico de Sevilla
listings.content: It has one of the best collection of Roman-era artifacts in Spain, brought from nearby Italica.

listings.name: Museo Antiquarium
listings.content: A museum with excavated Roman and Moorish remains, discovered during construction of the Metropol Parasol. You can enter for free if you show your ticket for the alcazar, even if the ticket is a few days old.

listings.name: Centro Andaluz de Arte Contempraneo
listings.content: Contemporary art museum in the former Carthusian monastery of Santa Maria of Las Cuevas, which has a fascinating history as a clay mine, monastery, and ceramics factory. The site and expansive grounds are worth a visit in their own right, including a striking rose window, industrial chimneys, and orange orchards. This was one of the places where the remains of Christopher Columbus were buried, before ending up in the Cathedral.
listings.price: Visit monument €1.80; Temporary exhibitions €1.80; Complete Visit €3.01. Free on Tu-Fr 19:00-21:00 Sa 11:00-21:00

listings.name: Museo del Baile Flamenco
listings.content: Offers an experience for all the senses with ambiental music, videos, touch-screens and artifacts to be found in this 18th century building at the heart of the historical Barrio Santa Cruz. On Friday and Saturday evenings a spectacular show is hosted at a discounted price for visitors to the museum. Flamenco art and photography exhibitions are also on display and dance, singing, percussion and guitar lessons are offered.
listings.price: Museum: €10 adult, €8 senior, €6 child; performances: €20 adults, €14 senior, €12 child
listings.image: La noche larga de los Museos.jpg

listings.name: La Casa del Flamenco
listings.content: A good spot to see real flamenco.

listings.name: La Carbonería
listings.content: Offers free flamenco shows nightly. Arrive early for good seats.

listings.name: Semana Santa
listings.content: The sombre Easter week processions feature thousands of people and go on all week, a spectacular display of conspicuous Catholicism.

listings.name: Feria de Abril
listings.content: Also known as "Feria de Sevilla" - a release after the somberness of Semana Santa. To say this is a huge party would be an understatement. Most if not all of Seville takes a week's holiday (the Wednesday of Feria week is a public holiday) and they plan for the fair months in advance. The fair is close to the river. It covers a huge area and contains hundreds of private and public casetas which are laid out to form streets. Casetas are small marquees and you can only get into the private ones if invited. The public ones are large but just as much fun. The day is naturally split in two and between 12:00 and 20:00 the streets of the fair throng with horses as riders and carriages strut their stuff dressed in traditional Spanish robes. After 20:00 the streets are cleared and "Calle del Inferno" comes to life. This must be one of the best funfairs in Europe – it takes weeks to assemble and pack up. Experience traditional dress, flamenco dancing (and the "sevillanas", the traditional dance of the region of Seville), guitars, fino, great tapas and participants who dance with gusto and eat and drink the day and night away.

listings.name: Real Betis
listings.content: Capacity 60,700. Their women's team play in Liga F (their top tier) at the nearby Luis del Sol training ground.

listings.name: Sevilla FC
listings.content: Capacity 42,500. Their women's team play in Liga F at Ramón Cisneros training ground 5 km southeast of the centre.

listings.name: Plaza de Toros de la Real Maestranza
listings.content: Bullfighting is not a sport for all; those who are either squeamish or have convictions on animal welfare should stay clear, as the event concludes with the killing of the bulls. Failing that, a visit to the arena and the attached museum of bull-fighting is well worth the time. While it is not the largest, it is considered the most attractive bull arena in Spain due to its history.
listings.price: €7 adult, €4 senior or student, €3 child 7-11, free for child under 6; free on M 15:00-19:00

listings.name: Bodeguita Romero
listings.content: A classic neighbourhood bodega, very popular with locals and serving excellent tapas.

listings.name: El Librero Tapas y Quesos
listings.content: Does cheese dishes, ham dishes, tapas, menu del dia, etc. Very popular with locals.
listings.address: Pasaje de Andreu 4, Barrio de Santa Cruz

listings.name: Los Coloniales
listings.content: This tapas place is cozy and has only a few tables. Go there early to put your name on the board to get a table, then head inside for a couple of beers. Portions are large and food is very very good. Nice homemade desserts, too.

listings.name: Duo Tapas
listings.content: This bar offers a nice atmosphere and good food. The price is average and the size of the tapas is fair, but it may be crowded, so it's better not to go in a hurry, as you may need to wait for a table.

listings.name: Naturalmente
listings.content: Breakfast and lunch every day, with early dinner two nights a week - handy if you want to eat earlier than typical Spanish dining hours. The menu has a wide choice of breakfast "toasts", fruit and yoghurt bowls, cakes and pastries in the morning, changing to a range of lunch and dinner plates for lunch and dinner. There is a reasonable choice of vegan or vegetarian dishes, and overall the food is lighter than traditional Sevillian cuisine. The fruit juices are particularly tasty.

listings.name: Cafe-Bar Las Teresas
listings.content: A lively slice of ham heaven. Tourists and locals. If the sight of dead hogs hanging from the rafters offends you -- drink and eat elsewhere.

listings.name: Restaurante Fez
listings.content: Maroccan cuisine. Since you need a break from tapas. There are lots of other places serving Arabic food.

listings.name: Habanita
listings.content: In the centre of the city. Quiet open air restaurant with a very good selection of vegetarian and vegan foods.

listings.name: El Rinconcillo
listings.content: The oldest tavern around, try the Espinacas con Garbanzos (spinach with chickpeas) and Salmorejo, while watching the witty bartenders running around and writing your bill on the bar in front of you with, get this, chalk.

listings.name: Parcería Café
listings.content: Situated near Mercado Feria, Parcería is a tiny café serving coffee from a local roaster. Laptops aren’t allowed, but the coffee is worth a walk from the city centre.

listings.name: Utopía Café
listings.content: Hidden in a side street, Utopía is a takeaway-only café serving coffee from the same local roaster as Parcería.

listings.name: Delatribu
listings.content: A small takeaway café serving organic coffee and homemade pastry.

listings.name: CafeTeaTe
listings.content: Located inside the Triana market, this café also serves breakfast sandwiches and other items. Their espresso shots are slightly longer than one might expect, but still decent. Make sure to ask about the current coffees when you order, they usually have one darker and one lighter roast.
listings.address: Plaza del Altozano s/n Mercado de Triana, puesto 34-35

listings.name: B&B Naranjo
listings.content: Budget hotel in old house near bus station, rooms are small with some on third floor, no elevator. Pleasant rooftop terrace. The a/c struggles in hot weather.

listings.name: Oasis Backpackers' Hostel
listings.content: Clean friendly hostel with rooftop pool. Daily activities such as walking tours, Spanish classes, bar games.

listings.name: Oasis Backpackers' Palace Seville
listings.content: Dorms in all sizes, lockers to put your backpack in and free linen. Roof-top terrace with chill-out bar to overlook Seville, guest kitchen, free breakfast and free internet/ wifi.

listings.name: Sevilla Inn
listings.content: Great location 100 m east of Giralda. Spacious terrace with views of the cathedral.

listings.name: Triana Hostel
listings.content: Clean well-run hostel, painted ceramic tiles, and green plants among cozy sofas. Nice roof terrace with hammocks. Rooms are average-small for a hostel with creaky iron bunk beds, safety boxes and short of space. Free breakfast and 3 (slow) computers with internet access. It's 3 blocks from the river in a nice neighbourhood with narrow streets and old houses.

listings.name: Pension Vergara
listings.content: Simple pension but in a converted 15th-century convent.
listings.address: Calle Ximenez de Enciso 11, Barrio de Santa Cruz

listings.name: Hotel Pasarela
listings.content: Clean friendly place just behind the big plaza.

listings.name: Hostal Callejón del Agua
listings.content: Basic hotel, great location, very small rooms, street noise can be a problem.

listings.name: Hotel Abanico
listings.content: 22-room hotel in 18th century town house, small rooms but value for money, good location. Watch your step as you come out as traffic hurtles along the narrow street.

listings.name: Hotel Abril
listings.content: In a quiet street near Encarnacion Square 500 m north of centre. Small and simple hotel but clean, comfy and good value for money.

listings.name: Hotel Bellavista Sevilla
listings.content: Mid-range out-of-town hotel opposite hospital complex with 104 rooms with a/c. Has a café with outdoor terrace and à la carte restaurant, 24 hours reception, meeting rooms, pool and parking. Pets are allowed though some visitors have had problems over this.

listings.name: Hotel Itaca
listings.content: Small hotel north of centre, tiny rooms, several are blind. Mostly clean and comfy but they get a lot of street noise.

listings.name: Hotel Las Casas de los Mercaderes
listings.content: Comfy 3-star in great location 300 m north of Giralda. Some street noise, and don't bring a car to this pedestrianised area.

listings.name: Hotel Monte Carmelo
listings.content: Efficient modern hotel, 10 min walk to Plaza de España.

listings.name: Hotel Monte Triana
listings.content: Simple hotel, clean and friendly, has parking.
listings.address: Calle Clara de Jesús Montero, Triana

listings.name: Hotel Murillo
listings.content: Small, clean friendly place in the Juderia. Small rooms and sometimes noisy but value for money.

listings.name: NH Plaza de Armas
listings.content: Efficient modern hotel on west side of city centre. Rooftop pool, Wi-Fi, meeting rooms and a restaurant.

listings.name: NH Viapol Hotel
listings.content: Modern hotel 1 km east of old city, airport bus and other transport stops just outside.

listings.name: Hotel San Gil
listings.content: 4-star going on 3, gets mixed reviews for comfort and service, 1 km north of city centre. Small rooftop pool and sun terrace.

listings.name: Singular Apartments
listings.content: Fully equipped apartments in 3 locations with large rooms and kitchens, also well suited for families or small groups.

listings.name: Casa Romana
listings.content: Comfy hotel 1 km north of city centre.

listings.name: Eme Catedral Hotel
listings.content: Comfy hotel in great location facing Giralda.

listings.name: Gran Melia Colón
listings.content: Plush hotel with spa, garage, restaurants and bars.

listings.name: Hotel Alfonso XIII
listings.content: Destination hotel, built for the Exposición in 1929, and converted into fabulous accommodation with prices to match. Has an outdoor pool, fitness centre, sauna and restaurant. Free Wi-Fi, public parking €22/day. Now part of Marriott.
listings.image: Hotel Alfonso XIII, Sevilla, España, 2015-12-06, DD 80.JPG

listings.name: Hotel Villa de la Palmera
listings.content: In an affluent section of Seville just outside the centre city of the city. The hotel is a former private home of the Marquis and Marquise of Castilleja, built in the early 20th century and renovated for use as a hotel in 1999. Services and amenities include breakfast and room service, pool, gardens and a terrace, free parking and free Wi-Fi internet access.

listings.name: Las Casas de la Judería
listings.content: Upscale hotel next to a former synagogue. Splurge if you can on a suite, these are in the exquisite main building. Other rooms are in some three dozen nearby houses, pleasant enough but lacking the wowie-zowie factor.

places.title: Alameda de Hércules
places.blurb: The Alameda de Hércules, or simply La Alameda, is a garden square or mall in Seville, southern Spain.

places.title: Alamillo Bridge
places.blurb: The Alamillo Bridge is a structure in Seville, Andalucia, which spans the Canal de Alfonso XIII, allowing access to La Cartuja, a peninsula located between the canal and the Guadalquivir River.

places.title: Birth of a New Man
places.blurb: Birth of a New Man, popularly known as el huevo de Colón, is a monument in Seville, Spain.

places.title: Archeological Museum of Seville
places.blurb: The Archeological Museum of Seville is a museum in Seville, southern Spain, housed in the Pabellón del Renacimiento, one of the pavilions designed by the architect Aníbal González.

places.title: Bellavista, Seville
places.blurb: Bellavista is a neighbourhood in the Bellavista-La Palmera district in the south of the city of Seville, Andalusia, Spain.

places.title: Alfalfa, Seville
places.blurb: Alfalfa is a neighbourhood in the historical centre of Seville, the Casco Antiguo.

places.title: Alamillo Park
places.blurb: Alamillo Park is a metropolitan park located between the town of Santiponce and Seville, Spain.

places.title: Seville Cathedral
places.blurb: The Cathedral of Saint Mary of the See, better known as Seville Cathedral, is a Catholic cathedral in Seville, Andalusia, Spain.

places.title: Estadio Benito Villamarín
places.blurb: Estadio Benito Villamarín is a stadium in Seville, Spain, and the home of Real Betis since its completion in 1929.

places.title: Torre del Oro
places.blurb: The Torre del Oro is a dodecagonal military watchtower in Seville, southern Spain.

places.blurb: The Plaza de España is a plaza in Maria Luisa Park in Seville, Spain.

places.title: Isla Mágica
places.blurb: Isla Mágica is a theme park at the Isla de La Cartuja, in Seville, Andalusia in Spain.

places.title: Santa Cruz, Seville
places.blurb: Santa Cruz, is the primary tourist neighborhood of Seville, Spain, and the former Jewish quarter of the medieval city.

places.title: El Arenal, Seville
places.blurb: El Arenal is a neighbourhood in the historical centre of Seville, the Casco Antiguo.

places.title: Palace of the Countess of Lebrija
places.blurb: The Lebrija Palace or Palacio de la Condesa de Lebrija is a house museum in central Seville, Spain.

places.title: Museum of Fine Arts of Seville
places.blurb: The Museum of Fine Arts of Seville is one of the main art galleries in Seville, Spain, with a collection of Spanish visual arts from the medieval period to the early 20th century.

places.title: Monastery of Santa Maria de las Cuevas
places.blurb: The Monastery of Santa María de las Cuevas, also known as the Monastery of the Cartuja, is a religious building on the Isla de La Cartuja in Seville, southern Spain.

places.title: Teatro de la Maestranza
places.blurb: The Teatro de la Maestranza is an opera house located in Seville, Spain.

places.title: Museum of Arts and Popular Customs of Seville
places.blurb: The Museum of Arts and Popular Customs of Seville is a museum in Seville, Andalusia, Spain, located in the María Luisa Park, across the Plaza de América from the Provincial Archeological Museum.

places.title: Casa de Pilatos
places.blurb: La Casa de Pilatos is an Andalusian palace in Seville, Spain, which serves as the permanent residence of the Dukes of Medinaceli.

places.title: Torre de la Plata
places.blurb: The Torre de la Plata is an octagonal military tower in Andalusia, located in present-day Seville, southern Spain.

places.title: Santa María Magdalena, Seville
places.blurb: Santa María Magdalena is a Baroque church in Seville, southern Spain.

places.title: Parque de María Luisa
places.blurb: The Parque de María Luisa is a public park that stretches along the Guadalquivir River in Seville, Spain.

places.title: Monastery of San Isidoro del Campo
places.blurb: The Monastery of San Isidoro del Campo is a monastery located in Santiponce, Spain.

places.title: Church of Santa Catalina
places.blurb: The Church of Santa Catalina is a church located in Sevilla, Spain, constructed in the fourteenth century.

places.title: Plaza de América
places.blurb: The Plaza de América, located in the Parque de María Luisa, was built by architect Aníbal González for the Ibero-American exhibition of 1929.

places.title: Puente de Isabel II
places.blurb: The Puente de Isabel II, Puente de Triana or Triana Bridge, is a metal arch bridge in Seville, Spain, that connects the Triana neighbourhood with the centre of the city.

places.title: Castle of San Jorge
places.blurb: The Castle of San Jorge was a medieval fortress built on the west bank of the Guadalquivir river in the Spanish city of Seville.

places.title: Caños de Carmona
places.blurb: The Caños de Carmona is a Roman aqueduct built during the first century BC to supply water from a spring in the ancient Roman city of Irippo –current Alcalá de Guadaíra– to the ancient Roman city of Hispalis –current…

places.title: Monastery of San Clemente
places.blurb: Monastery of San Clemente is a Cistercian monastery with the Bien de Interés Cultural designation in the Spanish city of Seville.

places.title: Plaza Nueva, Seville
places.blurb: Plaza Nueva is a public square in the city center of Seville, Spain, containing the Seville City Hall.

places.title: FIBES Conference and Exhibition Centre
places.blurb: The Conference and Exhibition Centre of Seville, usually referred to as FIBES or Fibes, is a conference and exhibition centre in Seville, Andalusia, Spain.

places.title: Roman amphitheatre of Italica
places.blurb: The Roman amphitheatre of Italica is a Roman amphitheatre in the Roman colonia of Italica –in present-day Santiponce, Spain–, in the Roman province of Hispania Baetica.

places.title: Monumento a la Raza
places.blurb: The Monumento a la Raza is an outdoor marble monument in the city of Seville, Andalusia, Spain.

places.title: Buhaira Gardens
places.blurb: The Buhaira Gardens, also known as the Buhaira Palace or the Buḥayra, is a former Almohad garden and palace in Seville, Spain.
